books.name: The Band's Commas
books.focus: who / which: extra information (commas) or needed information (no commas)

items.s: Kenji___ who plays the drums, is joining our band.
items.tip: Extra information about a named person goes between two commas: Kenji, who plays the drums, is…

no.no mark: There's a closing comma after drums, so the extra information needs an opening comma too.
no.;: A semicolon joins two full sentences, and Kenji on its own isn't one.
no.:: A colon introduces a list or an explanation. Here we're just adding extra information about Kenji.

items.say: Kenji, who plays the drums, is joining our band.
items.ask: Kenji who plays the drums, is joining our band.

items.s: The girl___ who sings in our band is my cousin.
items.tip: who sings in our band tells us WHICH girl. Needed information takes no commas.

no.,: who sings in our band tells us which girl we mean. The sentence needs it, so no comma.
no.;: A semicolon joins two full sentences. The girl isn't a full sentence.
no.:: A colon introduces a list or an explanation. Here there's nothing to introduce.

items.say: The girl who sings in our band is my cousin.
items.ask: The girl who sings in our band is my cousin.

items.s: Our band room___ which used to be a storeroom, is tiny.
items.tip: which adds extra information, so it goes between two commas.

no.no mark: There's a closing comma after storeroom, so the extra part needs an opening comma too.
no.;: A semicolon would cut off Our band room, which isn't a full sentence.
no.:: A colon introduces a list or an explanation. Here we just add a fact about the room.

items.say: Our band room, which used to be a storeroom, is tiny.
items.ask: Our band room which used to be a storeroom, is tiny.

items.s: The song___ that we wrote last week is called Moonlight.
items.tip: that we wrote last week tells us which song. Needed information never takes commas, and that never follows a comma here.

no.,: that we wrote last week tells us which song. Needed information has no commas, and that doesn't come after a comma.
no.;: A semicolon joins two full sentences. The song isn't a full sentence.
no.:: A colon introduces something. Here we just say which song.

items.say: The song that we wrote last week is called Moonlight.
items.ask: The song that we wrote last week is called Moonlight.

items.s: My guitar___ which I got for my birthday, is purple.
items.tip: You have one guitar, so which I got for my birthday is extra information: put it between commas.

no.no mark: There's a closing comma after birthday, so the extra information needs an opening comma too.
no.;: A semicolon joins two full sentences. My guitar isn't one.
no.:: A colon introduces a list or an explanation. Here we just add a fact.

items.say: My guitar, which I got for my birthday, is purple.
items.ask: My guitar which I got for my birthday, is purple.

items.s: Anyone___ who wants to join can come to the audition.
items.tip: who wants to join tells us which people. Needed information: no commas.

no.,: who wants to join tells us WHO can come. The sentence needs it, so no comma.
no.;: A semicolon joins two full sentences. Anyone isn't a full sentence.
no.:: A colon introduces something. Here we just say which people.

items.say: Anyone who wants to join can come to the audition.
items.ask: Anyone who wants to join can come to the audition.

items.s: Our music teacher___ Ms Lee, gave us some great tips.
items.tip: Ms Lee is the teacher's name, added as extra information between two commas.

no.no mark: There's a closing comma after Lee, so her name needs an opening comma too.
no.;: A semicolon would cut off Our music teacher, which isn't a full sentence.
no.:: A colon introduces a list or an explanation. Here we just add her name.

items.say: Our music teacher, Ms Lee, gave us some great tips.
items.ask: Our music teacher Ms Lee, gave us some great tips.

items.s: The concert___ which was in the school hall, sold out in a day.
items.tip: which was in the school hall is extra information about the concert, so it goes between commas.

no.no mark: There's a closing comma after hall, so the extra part needs an opening comma too.
no.;: A semicolon joins two full sentences. The concert isn't one.
no.:: A colon introduces something. Here we just add where the concert was.

items.say: The concert, which was in the school hall, sold out in a day.
items.ask: The concert which was in the school hall, sold out in a day.

books.name: Colons on the Hike
books.focus: colon (:) to introduce · semicolon (;) to join two sentences

items.s: Pack three things for the hike___ a hat, a water bottle and sun cream.
items.tip: A colon introduces a list after a full sentence: Pack three things: a hat, …

no.;: A semicolon joins two full sentences, but a hat, a water bottle and sun cream isn't a sentence.
no.,: A comma here would make the list look like part of the first list.
no.no mark: Without a mark, the list runs straight into the sentence. A colon says 'here they are'.

items.say: Pack three things for the hike: a hat, a water bottle and sun cream.
items.ask: Pack three things for the hike a hat, a water bottle and sun cream.

items.s: The hike was long___ the view from the top made it worth it.
items.tip: A semicolon joins two full sentences that are closely linked.

no.,: A comma can't join two full sentences on its own (that's a comma splice).
no.:: A colon introduces an explanation or a list, but the view doesn't explain the long hike.
A full stop works only if the next word has a capital: The view…

items.say: The hike was long; the view from the top made it worth it.
items.ask: The hike was long the view from the top made it worth it.

items.s: There was only one problem___ we had forgotten the map!
items.tip: A colon introduces an explanation: what was the problem? We had forgotten the map.

no.;: A semicolon links two equal sentences, but here the second part explains 'one problem', which is a colon's job.
no.,: A comma can't join two full sentences.
no.no mark: Two full sentences can't just run together.

items.say: There was only one problem: we had forgotten the map!
items.ask: There was only one problem we had forgotten the map!

items.s: Aisha loves climbing___ her brother prefers swimming.
items.tip: A semicolon joins two full sentences about the same thing (here, a contrast).

no.,: A comma alone can't join two full sentences.
no.:: A colon introduces an explanation, but swimming doesn't explain Aisha's climbing.
no.no mark: Two full sentences can't just run together.

items.say: Aisha loves climbing; her brother prefers swimming.
items.ask: Aisha loves climbing her brother prefers swimming.

items.s: We needed just one more thing___ a torch.
items.tip: A colon introduces the thing you've been waiting for: a torch.

no.;: A semicolon needs a full sentence on both sides, and a torch isn't a sentence.
no.,: A comma is too weak here. The colon points to what the 'one more thing' is.
no.!: ! would end the sentence before we find out what we needed.

items.say: We needed just one more thing: a torch.
items.ask: We needed just one more thing a torch.

items.s: It rained all morning___ by lunchtime, the sky had cleared.
items.tip: Two full, linked sentences can be joined with a semicolon.

no.,: A comma alone can't join two full sentences.
no.:: A colon introduces an explanation, but a clear sky doesn't explain the rain.

items.say: It rained all morning; by lunchtime, the sky had cleared.
items.ask: It rained all morning by lunchtime, the sky had cleared.

items.s: The rules were simple___ stay together and stay on the path.
items.tip: A colon introduces what the rules are.

no.;: A semicolon needs a full sentence on both sides. Here the second part explains the rules, which is a colon's job.
no.,: A comma can't introduce the rules. A colon says 'here they are'.
no.no mark: Without a mark, the rules crash into the sentence.

items.say: The rules were simple: stay together and stay on the path.
items.ask: The rules were simple stay together and stay on the path.

items.s: Some of us were tired___ others wanted to keep going.
items.tip: A semicolon links two full sentences that contrast: Some…; others…

no.,: A comma alone can't join two full sentences.
no.:: A colon introduces an explanation, but the second part doesn't explain the first.
no.no mark: Two full sentences can't just run together.

items.say: Some of us were tired; others wanted to keep going.
items.ask: Some of us were tired others wanted to keep going.

books.name: Game Night Questions
books.focus: question tags · reported and polite questions · interrupted speech

items.s: This game is brilliant___ isn't it?
items.tip: Put a comma before a question tag: …, isn't it?

A full stop would leave isn't it? on its own.
no.?: The question mark goes at the very end, after the tag.
no.;: A semicolon joins two full sentences. isn't it is a tag, not a sentence.

items.say: This game is brilliant, isn't it?
items.ask: This game is brilliant isn't it?

items.s: She asked me where the controller was___
items.tip: A reported question tells us what someone asked, so it ends with a full stop.

no.?: This is a reported question (She asked me where…). The sentence tells, it doesn't ask, so a full stop.
no.,: A comma can't end a sentence.
no.!: Nothing is shouted here. It's a calm report.

items.say: She asked me where the controller was.
items.ask: She asked me where the controller was

items.s: “Have you finished level ten___” Sam asked.
items.tip: A direct question keeps its question mark inside the speech marks.

no.,: Have you finished…? is a real question, so it keeps its question mark even before Sam asked.
A full stop would end the sentence, and Sam is asking.
no.!: ! is for a shout. Sam is asking a question.

items.say: “Have you finished level ten?” Sam asked.
items.ask: “Have you finished level ten” Sam asked.

items.s: You haven't seen my headphones___ have you?
items.tip: Put a comma before a question tag: …, have you?

A full stop would leave have you? on its own.
no.?: The question mark goes at the very end, after the tag.
no.;: A semicolon joins two full sentences. have you is a tag.

items.say: You haven't seen my headphones, have you?
items.ask: You haven't seen my headphones have you?

items.s: I wonder whether the new update is out yet___
items.tip: I wonder whether… is a statement about your thoughts, so it ends with a full stop.

no.?: I wonder whether… isn't a direct question. It tells us what you're thinking, so it takes a full stop.
no.,: A comma can't end a sentence.
no.!: Nothing here is a shout or a big feeling.

items.say: I wonder whether the new update is out yet.
items.ask: I wonder whether the new update is out yet

items.s: The two ___ scores are on the big screen.
items.tip: Two players = plural ending in s, so the apostrophe goes after the s: players'.

no.player's: player's means one player, but there are two: players'.
no.players: players (no apostrophe) doesn't show that the scores belong to them.
no.players's: After a plural ending in s, add only the apostrophe: players'.

items.say: The two players' scores are on the big screen.
items.ask: The two players' scores are on the big screen.

items.s: “That's not fair___” complained my sister, “you had an extra life!”
items.tip: When one sentence of speech is split by complained my sister, the first part ends with a comma.

A full stop would end her sentence, but it carries on: “you had…” starts with a small y.
no.!: ! would end her sentence, but it carries on with a small y, so use a comma.
no.?: She isn't asking anything. She's complaining.

items.say: “That's not fair,” complained my sister, “you had an extra life!”
items.ask: “That's not fair” complained my sister, “you had an extra life!”

items.s: Could you tell me what time the tournament starts___
items.tip: Could you tell me…? is a polite question, so it ends with a question mark.

Could you tell me…? is still a question to someone, so it needs a question mark.
no.,: A comma can't end a sentence.
no.!: ! is for a shout. This is a polite question.

items.say: Could you tell me what time the tournament starts?
items.ask: Could you tell me what time the tournament starts
